title: prefill-vs-decode-pipeline-design
content:
Summary:
This doc proposes a unified approach to prefill vs decode pipeline design for Redwood's serving runtime. It covers overlap opportunities, micro-batching strategies, stream priority and scheduling, interactions with the KV cache, and kernel-level implications. Goal is to reduce end-to-end latency for streaming/interactive workloads while preserving throughput for batch workloads and keeping per-customer fairness and SLOs predictable.

Background and motivation:
- Modern decoder-only LLM inference has two natural phases: prefill (encode prompt / build KV cache for context) and decode (autoregressive token generation reading/writing KV cache).
- Prefill is often heavier (longer sequence length) and benefits from large micro-batches and fused kernels. Decode is latency-sensitive and benefits from small micro-batches / streaming.
- Many real workloads interleave prefill and decode (chat with little prefill, then streaming decode), and others require long prefill followed by fast decode. Overlapping prefill and decode work on the same GPU could improve utilization but introduces KV cache consistency, kernel switching, and scheduling complexity.

Goals:
- Minimize tail latency for interactive streaming decodes.
- Improve GPU utilization by overlapping prefill and decode when safe and beneficial.
- Keep predictable cost/throughput for reserved/dedicated customers.
- Maintain correctness: decode must read a stable KV cache for the tokens it consumes.

Terminology:
- Prefill: initial forward pass over input tokens to produce KV cache and final hidden state before autoregressive decoding.
- Decode step: a single autoregressive token generation iteration (KV read, attention, FCs, KV write).
- Micro-batch: grouping multiple requests/tokens to amortize kernel overhead.
- Stream: a logical request/connection producing a sequence of decode tokens.
- KV slice: contiguous memory for keys/values for a given stream/session.

High-level design options considered:
1) Strict separation (no overlap): prefill runs to completion, writes final KV, then decode starts. Simplest correctness model.
2) Pipelined overlap with per-stream locking: allow decode to start on streams whose prefill is complete while prefill for other streams continues.
3) Fine-grained interleaving: allow decode of early tokens while later prefill tokens are still being computed for the same stream (requires partial KV consistency guarantees).
4) Kernel-fused hybrid: dynamically switch kernels to favor long-sequence prefill vs single-step decode, with scheduler controlling kernel selection per micro-batch.

Recommended approach (2 + 4 hybrid):
- Allow pipeline overlap at stream granularity (option 2). A decode may execute for a stream only when that stream's prefill has produced the KV rows up to the tokens that the decode will consume. We do not attempt intra-stream partial decode (avoid option 3 complexity for now).
- Scheduler groups work into micro-batches that are homogeneous by phase (prefill vs decode) and similar sequence lengths, then uses kernel selection tuned for that phase.
- Where possible, co-schedule short prefill micro-batches with decode micro-batches to fill GPU slack, but enforce strict KV dependencies per stream.

KV cache model and consistency rules:
- KV cache is per-model/per-stream contiguous memory. Writes are append-only in sequence order for a stream.
- Each decode op specifies required KV depth (N): the number of past tokens it will read. The scheduler only schedules decode micro-batch for streams whose current KV depth >= N.
- Prefill writes increase KV depth; writes are ordered. No in-place mutation of previously written KV rows.
- Eviction and compaction: a background process may evict/compact oldest KV rows by stream; scheduler must consult active outstanding decodes to avoid evicting required rows.

Micro-batching strategy:
- Prefill micro-batches: batch by similar prompt lengths and by client-level affinity (same model, same quantization). Target larger batches to amortize compute and kernel startup costs. Allow larger workspace for fused attention.
- Decode micro-batches: prefer small batches to reduce per-token latency. Batch streams waiting for the same next token with a small timeout (configurable, e.g., 3-10ms) and a max batch size.
- Adaptive thresholds: scheduler monitors latency SLOs and GPU utilization. If utilization is low, relax decode timeouts to form larger decode micro-batches. If latency SLOs degrade, tighten decode timeouts.
- Micro-batch tags: every micro-batch is tagged with phase (PREFILL/DECODE), model, quantization, kernel_hint, and priority. Scheduler groups on these tags.

Stream priorities and scheduling policy:
- Priority levels: REALTIME (low token budgets, interactive authors), STANDARD (default), BACKGROUND (bulk/async).
- Queueing: maintain separate queues per priority and phase. Use weighted round-robin across priorities with token-based shaping so BACKGROUND cannot starve REALTIME.
- Preemption: allow decode micro-batch preemption for higher-priority real-time streams if a decode is queued and GPU is free for > max_idle_ms. Preemption is at micro-batch boundary; we do not preempt running kernels.
- Admission control: refuse or re-route prefill-heavy requests when they would violate SLOs for higher priority streams (route to Dedicated, fall back to smaller model, or enqueue with lower priority).

Kernel selection and execution implications:
- Kernels tuned for prefill: fused multi-head-attention over long sequences, high memory throughput, larger GEMM tiling.
- Kernels tuned for decode: single-step KV read/write optimized kernels with low kernel-launch overhead and fused matmuls for small batch sizes.
- Runtime maintains multiple kernel implementations and a simple cost model. Scheduler picks kernel_hint per micro-batch.
- Kernel switching cost: switching kernels can involve reconfiguring workspace and buffers. Minimize switches by coalescing similar micro-batches. Short-lived decode bursts should use low-overhead kernels even if slightly less FLOP-efficient.

KV memory & placement concerns:
- Prefill benefits from contiguous KV placement to enable fused attention and streaming writes. Decodes benefit from low-latency random KV reads.
- Consider a memory layout with per-layer dense KV pages plus a small L1-like KV cache for hot recent rows to accelerate decode reads. Eviction policy LRU per-stream with protection window = in-flight decode depth.

Failure modes and correctness:
- If prefill fails mid-write: mark stream as failed and invalidate corresponding KV depth. Decodes dependent on that KV must be aborted or restarted.
- Race conditions guarded by per-stream sequence numbers and atomic write pointers. Scheduler validates KV depth before enqueueing decode micro-batches.

Observability and metrics to add:
- Per-stream: KV depth, time to first decode, avg decode latency, tokens/sec (decode), prefill duration, kernel type used.
- Per-GPU: micro-batch mix ratio (prefill vs decode), kernel-switch frequency, average kernel latency, idle tail (time GPU is idle waiting for high-priority decode).
- SLO alerts: 95/99th decode latency per priority, burst queuing time, prefill queuing time.

Experiments to run (priority ordered):
1) Baseline: strict separation implementation to establish prefill-first decode-later performance.
2) Per-stream overlap: allow decode to run for streams with completed prefill. Measure tail latency and GPU utilization.
3) Co-schedule prefills and decodes with small coalescing time windows; measure kernel switch overhead and throughput.
4) Introduce adaptive decode timeout and measure 95/99th token latency vs throughput tradeoff.
5) Implement small L1 KV cache for hot recent rows and measure reduction in decode latency for short-history decodes.

Implementation plan (milestones):
- Phase 1 (2 weeks): infra scaffolding: per-stream KV depth tracking, micro-batch metadata tags, baseline strict separation scheduler.
- Phase 2 (3 weeks): implement per-priority queues, decode batching timeout, and kernel selection hint plumbing.
- Phase 3 (3 weeks): per-stream overlap support and correctness checks, metrics. Run experiments 1-3.
- Phase 4 (4 weeks): L1 KV cache prototype, adaptive timeout policies, policy tuning, run experiments 4-5.

Open questions / decisions to make:
- Do we want to support partial-intra-stream decoding (decode while later prefill tokens are still being computed)? Higher utilization but complex correctness. Recommend deferring.
- How aggressive should eviction be for KV memory to balance multi-tenant memory pressure vs decode latency?
- What are sensible default timeouts for decode batching across latency-critical customers? (suggest 3-10ms but need experiments).

Next steps:
- Review with serving-runtime, SRE, and product (hosted API) for acceptability of admission control routes.
- Prioritize experiments and allocate GPUs for A/B testing.
- Add restful/internal API hooks for per-request priority and admission hints.
